title: Three bows
hook: one for the Buddha, one for the dhamma, one for the sangha; bowing as setting pride down

segments.voice: Yesterday, the home shrine: an image, a candle, incense, a flower, water, somewhere high and clean. Your line was a quiet corner. Did you clear a few inches of shelf? Day one hundred forty.

For some first-time visitors, bowing is the hardest part of a temple. Sitting in silence, fine. Chanting, sure. But a forehead on the cool temple floor? Something in the chest can go stiff. I don't bow to anyone. And that stiffness, Buddhist teachers would say, is exactly the point. The bow isn't about who's above you. It's about what you're carrying. Today: three bows, and what gets set down with them.
screen: `SILENCE, FINE. CHANTING, SURE.` → `FOREHEAD ON THE FLOOR?` → `WHAT ARE YOU CARRYING?`

segments.voice: In Theravada practice, people bow three times in front of the shrine, usually after the homage you learned two days ago. One bow for the Buddha, one for the dhamma, one for the sangha: the three refuges, in the body. The traditional bow is called the five-point bow. You kneel, sit back on your heels, bring your palms together at the chest, then lower yourself so that five points touch the floor: the forehead, the two forearms or hands, and the two knees. Then you come back up. Three times. The Pali word for this kind of respect is vandana. Other traditions bow differently. In Zen, people bow with palms together, a gesture called gassho in Japanese. In Tibetan Buddhism, practitioners may make full-length prostrations, stretching out flat on the floor, and some take them up as a whole practice of their own, counted out over months. Different forms, the same gesture: lowering the head. Why does that matter? Because the tradition names pride, mana in Pali, conceit, the sense of I am, as one of the last things to fall away on the whole path. The bow puts it down for a moment, on purpose, with the body. Your forehead, where the thinking seems to live, goes lower than your heart. Nobody is being worshiped as a god here. Buddhists say they're bowing to awakening, to the teaching, to the people who practice it, and to the possibility of those in themselves. Some teachers put it this way: an honest bow leaves a person lighter, not smaller, standing up with something heavy left on the floor.
screen: `ONE EACH: BUDDHA, DHAMMA, SANGHA.` · `FIVE POINTS TOUCH THE FLOOR.` · `GASSHO; FULL PROSTRATIONS.` · `MANA: PRIDE, SET DOWN.` · then, large: `BOW.`

segments.voice: If your body allows, kneel, or stay seated if that's better. Bring your palms together at the chest. Lower your head, as far as is comfortable, once for the Buddha, once for the dhamma, once for the sangha. Or if you'd rather, one for awakening, one for the truth, one for everyone walking toward it. Go slowly. Feel the head come lower than the heart. Then sit, and notice whatever is lighter. The bell holds the time.
Three bows. One for the Buddha, one for the dhamma, one for the sangha: the head lowered, pride set down for a moment.
Your line: bow. Today, bow three times, at a shrine, beside your bed, or just with a nod of the head, and notice what the stiffness in you says about it. Day one hundred forty.

howItsDone: Theravada Buddhists commonly bow three times with the five-point bow before a shrine or a monk; Zen practitioners bow with palms together, and Tibetan Buddhists may make full-length prostrations.

match.prompt: match the bow to the tradition or meaning.
pairs: forehead, forearms and knees touch the floor

myth: the three bows are one each for the Buddha, the dhamma and the sangha
the three refuges, done with the body.
Buddhists bow because they worship the Buddha as a god
they describe it as respect for awakening, the teaching and those who practice it.
the tradition names pride as one of the last things to fall away on the path
mana, conceit, is among the last fetters.

fork.setup: you're kneeling at a shrine for the first time. how many points of the body touch the floor in the traditional Theravada bow?
fork.reveal: it's the five-point bow: forehead, both forearms or hands, and both knees, three times over.

original.note: Pali: homage, respectful salutation, including the bow; also the name of the chanting that goes with it.

trapdoor: what you thought: bowing means submitting to someone above you.
what it means: setting pride down with the body, one bow for each of the three jewels.
what a scholar hears: mana (conceit) is one of the fetters said to be abandoned only at full awakening, so the humble bow points at the very end of the path.

sources.ref: Mana as one of the ten fetters (e.g. Samyutta Nikaya 45.180)

notes: The five-point bow (forehead, forearms/palms, knees) is described as commonly practiced in Theravada; confirm details.
The claim that mana (conceit) is abandoned only at arahantship (as one of the five higher fetters) should be confirmed, along with the citation.
Prostrations 'counted out over months' alludes to Tibetan ngondro preliminaries (traditionally 100,000); the exact number was cut from the voice under the claims rule.

Editor review (2026-10-01): hook no longer claims bowing is hardest 'for a lot of people' or tells the listener their chest goes stiff; cut the 'hundred thousand' count; 'teachers often notice' became 'some teachers put it this way'.
The hook's 'I don't bow to anyone' is the listener's inner voice, not the narrator's.
